I’ll read the continuation plan and the project’s established results first, then carry out the next research steps and save the progress, notes, and chat history in this investigation.

The plan starts with two concrete checks: extending the signed error estimates to physical heat time, and accounting for contour and cluster-coordinate errors. I’ll run those in parallel while comparing the two proposed transport mechanisms, then assess whether either provides a useful signed-cost bound.

The physical-time extension works with the existing constants, and the contour-transfer calculation stays regular when the pair merges. The remaining issue is the signed cost itself. I’m checking the finite Jacobi model’s exact heat-equation residual so that its motion can be compared fairly with direct contour bounds.

The finite-model calculation gives a useful warning: obtaining its exact heat residual requires the same extra coefficient that also makes the next Jacobi approximation available. The residual is much larger than that next approximation’s error. I’ll check whether this loss persists after signed contour integration near a hypothetical double event, rather than treating a large upper bound as a failure of the method.

The fixed-event calculation also works: under the stated hypothetical double-event assumption, the signed residual alternates with approximation degree, and the costly factor survives contour integration. It also gives a sharper location and uniqueness result for the nearby finite-model collision. These are conditional local results; they neither establish nor exclude a theta collision. I’m having that follow-through checked now.

The final proof check is passing so far. It caught one missing height restriction in the synthesis’s description of an older result; I’m correcting that and updating the records. No canonical tube or positive gap margin was acquired, so the numerical and slab-composition tasks remain unstarted.

The research round and its internal assessments are complete. The previous round left one useful question open: it measured a large residual term, but did not quantify its cancellation with the incoming error. I’ll investigate that joint quantity and compare one correction built from the signed quadrature error against the next finite model. Both comparisons will use the same coefficient information.

A concrete follow-up has emerged at time lengths of order \(N^{-2}\), where \(N\) is the model degree. This is larger than the earlier \(N^{-3}\) test: the roots move enough that their contribution to the quadrature error changes substantially. I’ll derive the incoming-error, residual, and drift contributions together. The simpler monomial correction already loses to the next model in the parent results, so I’ll retain that finding rather than repeat it.

The first calculations give explicit profiles for all three terms, and the separate drift calculation agrees with the profile obtained from the exact error identity. At the \(N^{-2}\) time scale, the drift contributes at the same leading order as the other terms, so dropping it would misstate the comparison. I’m checking the relative errors and the limits through the double root before recording this as a result.

The joint comparison now shows the cancellation explicitly. At one point on the backward-time scale, the three leading signed contributions are \(-1\), \(-2\), and \(4\): they sum to \(1\), while their absolute values sum to \(7\). Preserving that cancellation removes the overestimate from adding magnitudes, but the full correction still has the original model’s endpoint error. I’m preparing the proofs for a separate internal assessment.

The assessment has checked the main profiles and both time directions. It also prompted a clearer comparison: both errors are now explicitly measured at the same endpoint with the same weighting, and matching coefficient indices is distinguished from the cost of evaluating a whole time interval. The new drift formula also appears to resolve the smaller-time remainder left open in the first proof; I’m checking that short corollary before closing the round.

The smaller-time corollary checks out: the drift contribution is quadratic in the scaled interval length, while the residual contribution is linear. That connects the earlier \(N^{-3}\) calculation to the new \(N^{-2}\) analysis. I’m updating the progress register and continuation note to distinguish these conditional results from the still-unproved canonical gap estimate.

The research round is complete and internally assessed. The notes now cover the full cancellation, the direct drift calculation, and the smaller-time corollary. The progress register records what remains open: no canonical positive margin or collision exclusion has been obtained. I’m finishing the file checks and chat-history capture.

I’m selecting a canonical test around the classical Lehmer pair, whose two zeros are unusually close. The question is whether retaining the sign of the exterior drift gives a useful gap budget on a fixed positive-time interval where an absolute-value bound loses too much. I’ll compare it with direct evaluation at the same endpoint and distinguish numerical evidence from a certified bound.

The next step now has two parallel parts: proving an error bound for the complete-source evaluator and testing the signed gap budget on the fixed tube. The contour count and positive-time gap are acquisition targets; I’m not assuming them from the known time-zero pair.

The evaluator benchmark is practical: the two prescribed grids should take roughly five minutes of source evaluation. The analytic source-error bound also looks small enough for a useful diagnostic. The remaining questions are whether the contour isolates the pair and whether the signed budget beats the absolute-value budget after the errors are included.

The first grid gives a useful result: the signed budget leaves a positive gap margin of about **0.001115**, while the absolute-value budget loses about **0.04757**. Direct evaluation agrees with the transported endpoint value. These are still grid diagnostics. Since the exterior curvature varies little, I’m preparing a bounded certification step using one uniform upper bound for it.

The finer grid reproduces the same margin. I’m now checking whether those cached values can support a bound over the whole contour and time interval, without another source run. The proof step has supplied the interpolation error; the numerical step is testing count two, a zero-free collar, and a uniform negative upper bound for \(K\).

The certification run passed its full-domain checks. It gives a signed margin above **0.00058485** and a transported lower bound \(D(0)>0.00074052\). The absolute-value budget fails this test, and the quadratic collision control gives the required negative margin. I’m having the proof, implementation, and replay assessed before recording this as the local result.

The separate internal review reproduced every certificate result and found no mathematical or numerical defect. It also confirmed that missing or altered input data are rejected. I’m finishing the records with the comparison stated precisely: direct evaluation gets the same paid contour geometry and gives a tighter endpoint bound. The general canonical estimate remains open.

The notes now separate the certified margin, **greater than 0.00058487578**, from the finer diagnostic estimate, about 0.001115. They also record the remaining research gap: this pays one fixed canonical tube, but supplies neither a general bound across heights nor an advantage over direct endpoint evaluation.

The research cycle is complete and the records are updated. The replay, collision control, input-integrity checks, and document checks passed.
